# How to use AI to build a moving day checklist that covers everything you'll forget

> **In short:** You can use any AI assistant — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, Le Chat, DeepSeek, or whichever you already have — to brainstorm a moving checklist that catches the small, easy-to-forget tasks (forwarding mail, transferring prescriptions, returning library books). You'll end with a personalised, time-staged list saved somewhere you'll actually open on the day.

Moving is one of those tasks where the to-do list is longer than anyone expects, and the things people forget tend to be the small administrative ones — not the packing tape, but the kind of thing that causes a slow trickle of inconvenience for months afterwards. This guide walks you through using an AI assistant as a brainstorming partner to surface those items, then turning the result into a checklist you can actually use.

## Before you start
- **An AI assistant you can chat with in plain English.** Any major one works — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, Le Chat, DeepSeek. A free account is fine for this task.
- **A rough idea of your move date and where you're moving** (same town, new city, new country — the further, the more you'll need to think about).
- **A place to save the final list** — a notes app, a spreadsheet, or even a piece of paper. (Optional but strongly recommended; a list you don't save is a list you don't use.)
- **About 20–30 minutes**, ideally before the boxes start appearing.

## Step 1 — Open your AI assistant and describe your move

Open the assistant of your choice in your browser or in its app — you'll see a familiar chat screen with a message box at the bottom and an empty conversation above it. If you've used it before, look for a button labeled something like **"New chat"** or a small **+** icon to start a fresh conversation; an old chat can confuse the answers. In the message box, type one or two sentences about your situation — where you're moving, roughly when, and the kind of place — then send it.

💬 Example: "I'm moving from a two-bedroom apartment to a house about 30 miles away, in mid-October. It's just me and a cat."

You'll know it worked when the assistant replies with a short acknowledgement, usually one or two lines, and probably asks a clarifying follow-up — like how big your place is, or whether you're hiring movers.

## Step 2 — Ask the assistant to list what people forget when moving

Now type a follow-up that focuses the assistant on the small, easy-to-miss tasks rather than the obvious ones (packing tape, boxes — you already know those). Ask it to think like someone who's helped many people move. If your assistant has a **"thinking,"** **"research,"** or **"deep search"** toggle, turn it on for this prompt — the answer usually gets more thorough. If you don't see such a toggle, just send the prompt normally; you'll still get a useful list.

💬 Example: "Make a long list of small, easy-to-forget moving tasks that aren't about packing — administrative things like forwarding mail, transferring prescriptions, returning library books, updating your address with banks, and so on. Don't include obvious packing tasks. Be thorough — give me at least 20."

You'll know it worked when the assistant returns a list of around 15–30 items, most of which you probably hadn't thought of. If the list feels short (under 10), reply with "expand that — give me 30 more" — assistants almost always oblige.

## Step 3 — Personalise the list with your actual situation

This is the step that turns a generic list into yours. Read through the assistant's response and note which items apply to you — kids, pets, a car, a garden, regular subscriptions, a home office. Then send a short reply asking the assistant to redo the list, this time flagging which tasks matter most for your situation. You're essentially saying: "given what I told you, what's actually relevant?"

💬 Example: "I have a cat, I subscribe to three streaming services, I work from home, and I drive. Can you redo the list and put a star next to anything that especially applies to me? You can drop tasks that obviously don't apply."

You'll know it worked when the revised list reflects your real life — for example, pet vaccination records and car insurance address changes are likely starred, while "school enrolment" or "well water testing" probably isn't.

## Step 4 — Break the list into time stages

A flat list of 25 items is hard to act on. Ask the assistant to reorganise the same tasks by when they need to happen, using time stages: 8 weeks out, 4 weeks out, 2 weeks out, 1 week out, moving day, and the first week after. A staged list is dramatically easier to follow because you only look at the next two weeks' worth at any time. **If the assistant flattens the response into one block instead of using headings, paste your prompt again and add the word "headings" or "with clear stage labels"** — that usually fixes it.

💬 Example: "Please reorganise this into stages: 8 weeks before moving day, 4 weeks before, 2 weeks before, 1 week before, moving day itself, and the first week after. Put each stage as its own heading with tasks underneath."

You'll know it worked when the response shows clear headings for each time stage with relevant tasks grouped underneath each one.

## Step 5 — Ask for the contact details you'll need

Many tasks depend on who you contact, and that's where a generic checklist often goes quiet. Ask the assistant to suggest the typical places, services, or organisations to notify in each stage, and the kind of information each one usually needs from you — account number, old address, new address, move date. **Treat these as a starting set, not a final answer:** the assistant doesn't know your actual provider names, so anything specific (which electric company, which vet, which insurer) is up to you to confirm by searching online or checking your own records.

💬 Example: "For each task, tell me who I'd typically contact and what information I'd need to have ready — for example, account number, old address, new address, move date."

You'll know it worked when each task has a "who to contact" line and a "what you'll need" line next to it. **One honest caveat:** if your assistant declines to name specific companies (some are cautious about this), ask it instead for the *type* of organisation — "which utilities," "which government bodies" — and find the names yourself.

## Step 6 — Save the list somewhere you'll actually open

An AI-generated list only helps if you can find it the morning of the move. Copy the final response into your notes app, a spreadsheet, or a printed sheet — whichever you actually use. Tickable checkboxes beat paragraphs on a chaotic day, so ask the assistant to rewrite each task as a one-line, checkbox-style item grouped by stage. **If your notes app doesn't support checkbox formatting, just put a dash "-" in front of each task** — the visual structure is what matters.

💬 Example prompt to send: "Now turn the whole list into checkbox format, one task per line, grouped by stage. Make each line short enough to read at a glance."

You'll know it worked when you have a saved file, sheet, or printed page with each task as its own tickable line. If your phone has a calendar app, drop the stage deadlines in as reminders — that's the difference between a list you glance at and a list you actually use.

## Common mistakes
- **Trusting the list blindly.** AI assistants can suggest tasks that don't apply to you (a "drain the garden sprinkler system" item when you live in a studio) or miss local rules. Read each item once and delete what doesn't fit.
- **Forgetting to ask about timing.** If the assistant gives you everything in one flat list, you'll do it all in the last week and miss the tasks that need 30 days' notice — many utilities, mail forwarding, gym or subscription cancellations, and some address-change forms.
- **Saving it in the chat and never opening it again.** The whole point of a checklist is to come back to it. Save the list somewhere you'll actually see it on moving morning — a phone note, a printed page on the fridge, or a shared doc with a partner.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** The same trick works for any big piece of life admin — planning a wedding, prepping for a baby, sorting out year-end finances. Ask the AI to brainstorm what people forget, then personalise and stage the list. The pattern is reusable.
- **For your work or business:** If you help clients or customers move (real estate agents, relocation services, property managers), you can spin this into a reusable template by saving your favourite prompt as a starting point for each new client, then adjusting the personal details.
- **If you're just getting started:** Pick the AI assistant you already have an account with. Don't waste time choosing between them for this — they all handle a checklist prompt competently, and the time you'd spend picking is better spent actually moving.

## Try it now
Open your AI assistant right now and send this single message: "I'm moving in about six weeks. List 20 small, easy-to-forget moving tasks that aren't about packing boxes. Then organise them into stages: six weeks out, two weeks out, moving day, and the first week after." Take two minutes to read the reply — that's the moment the moving-day stress gets a little lighter.
